claim: Basement membranes are polymers of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins that underlie epithelia and surround organs in all animals.
source: Basement membranes are polymers of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins that underlie epithelia and surround organs in all animals (Yurchenco, 2011; Kelley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yurchenco, 2011 and Kelley et al., 2014

claim: The main constituent of basement membranes is Collagen IV, a helical trimer consisting of three α chains, capable of forming polymeric networks that interact with other ECM proteins.
source: Their main constituent is Collagen IV, a helical trimer consisting of three α chains, capable of forming polymeric networks that interact with other ECM proteins.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about basement membrane composition

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has emerged in recent years as an excellent model to study production of Collagen and other ECM proteins thanks to evolutionary conservation, powerful genetic tools and little genetic redundancy.
source: The fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster has emerged in recent years as an excellent model to study production of Collagen and other ECM proteins thanks to evolutionary conservation, powerful genetic tools and little genetic redundancy (Denef et al., 2008; Martinek et al., 2008; Bunt et al., 2010; Haigo and Bilder, 2011; Drechsler et al., 2013; Lerner et al., 2013; Na et al., 2013; Devergne et al., 2014; McCall et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies from 2008-2014

claim: Two Collagen IV chains exist in Drosophila, encoded by Collagen at 25C (Cg25C, α1 chain) and viking (vkg, α2 chain).
source: Two Collagen IV chains exist in Drosophila, encoded by Collagen at 25C (Cg25C, α1 chain) and viking (vkg, α2 chain).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Drosophila Collagen IV composition

claim: Apart from Collagen IV, BMs include Laminin, Nidogen and Perlecan, which are conserved from flies to humans.
source: Apart from Collagen IV, BMs include Laminin, Nidogen and Perlecan, which are conserved from flies to humans as well (Hynes, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hynes, 2012

claim: In the larva, the main source of Collagen IV is the adipocytes of the fat body.
source: In the larva, the main source of Collagen IV is the adipocytes of the fat body (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011), known for their role in lipid storage and metabolic regulation, but also as an active secretory tissue which produces serum proteins and clotting factors normally present in the hemolymph (insect blood).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011

claim: The fat body is a key effector of innate immunity, known to produce and secrete to the hemolymph large amounts of antimicrobial peptides in response to infections.
source: The fat body is also a key effector of innate immunity, known to produce and secrete to the hemolymph large amounts of antimicrobial peptides in response to infections (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007

claim: Secreted proteins like Collagen reach the extracellular space through a controlled series of membrane traffic events ensuring fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane.
source: Secreted proteins like Collagen reach the extracellular space through a controlled series of membrane traffic events ensuring fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about protein secretion mechanisms

claim: Membrane trafficking is a well-recognized driver of changes in cell shape and PM amount during morphogenesis.
source: Besides its role in cargo transport, membrane trafficking is a well-recognized driver of changes in cell shape and PM amount during morphogenesis (Lecuit and Pilot, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lecuit and Pilot, 2003

claim: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from membrane contributions from the secretory pathway.
source: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from membrane contributions from the secretory pathway (Lecuit and Wieschaus, 2000), endocytic membrane recycling (Pelissier et al., 2003; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Fabrowski et al., 2013) and microvillar PM elaborations (Figard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lecuit and Wieschaus, 2000

claim: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from endocytic membrane recycling.
source: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from membrane contributions from the secretory pathway (Lecuit and Wieschaus, 2000), endocytic membrane recycling (Pelissier et al., 2003; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Fabrowski et al., 2013) and microvillar PM elaborations (Figard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pelissier et al., 2003; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Fabrowski et al., 2013

claim: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from microvillar PM elaborations.
source: During blastoderm cellularization, fast directed PM growth results from membrane contributions from the secretory pathway (Lecuit and Wieschaus, 2000), endocytic membrane recycling (Pelissier et al., 2003; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Fabrowski et al., 2013) and microvillar PM elaborations (Figard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Figard et al., 2013

claim: Secretory transport of Collagen molecules requires carriers larger than regular COPII vesicles because of its large size.
source: Because of its large size, secretory transport of Collagen molecules requires carriers larger than regular COPII vesicles (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saito et al., 2009

claim: Collagen molecules undergo postranslational modification along the secretory pathway by numerous Collagen-modifying enzymes such as glycosidases, and lysyl- and prolyl-hydroxylases, required for trimer formation.
source: Also, Collagen molecules undergo postranslational modification along the secretory pathway by numerous Collagen-modifying enzymes such as glycosidases, and lysyl- and prolyl-hydroxylases, required for trimer formation (Myllyharju and Kivirikko, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Myllyharju and Kivirikko, 2004

claim: Prolyl-hydroxylation is essential for trimer formation, mediated in Drosophila by the prolyl-4-hydroxylase PH4αEFB.
source: Prolyl-hydroxylation in particular is essential for trimer formation, mediated in Drosophila by the prolyl-4-hydroxylase PH4αEFB (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011

claim: Unlike fibrilar Collagen I, which flies lack, Collagen IV is secreted in functional form and does not require extracellular cleavage of the N- and C-terminal propeptides.
source: Unlike fibrilar Collagen I, which flies lack, Collagen IV is secreted in functional form and does not require extracellular cleavage of the N- and C-terminal propeptides (Khoshnoodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khoshnoodi et al., 2008

claim: Fibrotic diseases are characterized by aberrant and excessive deposition of ECM due to persistent immune stimulation following diverse types of injuries.
source: Finally, because Collagen is resistant to most proteases, disposing of aggregates when they occur is highly problematic. Such is the case of fibrotic diseases, characterized by aberrant and excessive deposition of ECM due to persistent immune stimulation following diverse types of injuries (Wynn and Ramalingam, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wynn and Ramalingam, 2012

claim: In a variety of tissues such as the liver, skin, kidney or fat tissue, fibrosis disrupts tissue organization and increases matrix stiffness, affecting normal cell and tissue physiology.
source: In a variety of tissues such as the liver, skin, kidney or fat tissue, fibrosis disrupts tissue organization and increases matrix stiffness, affecting normal cell and tissue physiology (Hoffman et al., 2011; Friedman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 2011 and Friedman et al., 2013

claim: Loss of shibire and other endocytic genes leads to excess PM growth, which traps Collagen IV in the pericellular space.
source: We found that loss of Dynamin and other endocytic components causes pericellular trapping of outgoing Collagen IV due to dramatic cortex expansion when endocytic removal of PM is prevented.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Loss of negative Toll immune regulator Cactus causes pericellular Collagen deposits due to excess PM caused by increased secretion.
source: Deposits also form in the absence of negative Toll immune regulator Cactus, excess PM being caused in this case by increased secretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Trimeric Collagen accumulation, downstream of Toll or endocytic defects, activates a tissue damage response.
source: Finally, we show that trimeric Collagen accumulation, downstream of Toll or endocytic defects, activates a tissue damage response.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: shibire knock-down (shii) causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: shibire knock-down (shii), as well as expression of dominant negative Dynamin (ShiK44A) (Moline et al., 1999), caused Vkg accumulation in adipocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Moline et al., 1999 for the ShiK44A construct

claim: Expression of dominant negative Dynamin (ShiK44A) causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: shibire knock-down (shii), as well as expression of dominant negative Dynamin (ShiK44A) (Moline et al., 1999), caused Vkg accumulation in adipocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Moline et al., 1999 for the ShiK44A construct

claim: Antibody staining confirmed reduced Dynamin expression in shii cells.
source: In validation of the phenotype, antibody staining confirmed reduced Dynamin expression in shii cells, whereas the staining increased after Shi.K44A overexpression (Figure 1C), attesting to the sensitivity of the antibody.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Cg25C accumulates in shii adipocytes.
source: This staining revealed that Cg25C, same as Vkg, accumulates in shii adipocytes (Figure 1D), thus confirming Collagen IV accumulation in these cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The accumulation of Collagen IV occurs at the cell periphery, under a basement membrane surrounding the tissue in the wild type and which still forms in shii adipocytes.
source: The accumulation of Collagen IV occurs at the cell periphery, under a basement membrane surrounding the tissue in the wild type and which still forms in shii adipocytes (Figure 1D; see also Figure 3B later).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 3B

claim: shi1 and shi2 thermosensitive mutations caused Vkg accumulation in adipocytes when larvae grew at restrictive temperature.
source: Further validating the requirement of shibire in normal Collagen IV distribution, shi1 and shi2 thermosensitive mutations (Kim and Wu, 1990) also caused Vkg accumulation in adipocytes when larvae grew at restrictive temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Kim and Wu, 1990 for the mutations

claim: Loss of Rab5 causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: In addition to Dynamin, a number of hits showing a similar peripheral Collagen IV accumulation phenotype in the screening turned out to encode components of the endocytic machinery as well, such as Rab5 (Figure 1E), Clathrin heavy chain (Figure 1F), the Rab5-GAP RN-Tre, the AP-2 components AP-2α and AP-2μ and Hrs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that defective endocytosis was indeed the cause for the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Loss of Clathrin heavy chain causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: In addition to Dynamin, a number of hits showing a similar peripheral Collagen IV accumulation phenotype in the screening turned out to encode components of the endocytic machinery as well, such as Rab5 (Figure 1E), Clathrin heavy chain (Figure 1F), the Rab5-GAP RN-Tre, the AP-2 components AP-2α and AP-2μ and Hrs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that defective endocytosis was indeed the cause for the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Loss of RN-Tre causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: In addition to Dynamin, a number of hits showing a similar peripheral Collagen IV accumulation phenotype in the screening turned out to encode components of the endocytic machinery as well, such as Rab5 (Figure 1E), Clathrin heavy chain (Figure 1F), the Rab5-GAP RN-Tre, the AP-2 components AP-2α and AP-2μ and Hrs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that defective endocytosis was indeed the cause for the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of AP-2α and AP-2μ causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: In addition to Dynamin, a number of hits showing a similar peripheral Collagen IV accumulation phenotype in the screening turned out to encode components of the endocytic machinery as well, such as Rab5 (Figure 1E), Clathrin heavy chain (Figure 1F), the Rab5-GAP RN-Tre, the AP-2 components AP-2α and AP-2μ and Hrs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that defective endocytosis was indeed the cause for the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of Hrs causes Vkg accumulation in adipocytes.
source: In addition to Dynamin, a number of hits showing a similar peripheral Collagen IV accumulation phenotype in the screening turned out to encode components of the endocytic machinery as well, such as Rab5 (Figure 1E), Clathrin heavy chain (Figure 1F), the Rab5-GAP RN-Tre, the AP-2 components AP-2α and AP-2μ and Hrs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that defective endocytosis was indeed the cause for the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The amount of Collagen IV present in destination BMs is reduced in endocytic defect conditions.
source: Concurrent with the accumulation of Collagen IV in the adipocytes producing it, we found that the amount of Collagen IV present in destination BMs (Figure 1G) and in the hemolymph (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) was reduced in these conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The amount of Collagen IV present in the hemolymph is reduced in endocytic defect conditions.
source: Concurrent with the accumulation of Collagen IV in the adipocytes producing it, we found that the amount of Collagen IV present in destination BMs (Figure 1G) and in the hemolymph (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) was reduced in these conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Elongation of the ventral nerve cord occurs in endocytic defect conditions.
source: In agreement with this, we observed elongation of the ventral nerve cord (Figure 1H), a deformation associated with Collagen IV reduction (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011 for the association with Collagen IV reduction

claim: Accumulations of Collagen IV in shii adipocytes are found in close proximity to the PM.
source: Accumulations of Collagen IV in shii adipocytes were found in close proximity to the PM, as revealed by the membrane marker myr-mRFP (myristoylation domain of Src fused to mRFP; Figure 2A) and by phalloidin staining of F-actin, normally enriched in the cell cortex (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B

claim: Short incubation with FM4-64 showed that the accumulations were surrounded by PM.
source: To determine whether Collagen IV accumulations were intracellular or extracellular we stained shii adipocytes with the lipophilic, cell-impermeable dye FM4-64 (Bolte et al., 2004) to label membrane directly in contact with the extracellular space (PM). Short incubation with FM4-64 showed that the accumulations were surrounded by PM (Figure 2C) and, thus, likely extracellular.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Bolte et al., 2004 for the FM4-64 dye

claim: Labeling of membrane around the accumulations was equally observed when shii adipocytes were fixed and stained with fluorescently-labeled fixable dextrans of molecular weights 70,000 and 3000.
source: Labeling of membrane around the accumulations was equally observed when shii adipocytes were fixed and stained with fluorescently-labeled fixable dextrans of molecular weights 70,000 (Figure 2D) and 3000 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Intracellularly retained Collagen IV in Tango1i adipocytes could not be stained without permeabilization.
source: To confirm that the Collagen IV accumulations in shii adipocytes were extracellular, we performed antibody stainings without permeabilizing the cells (no detergent in washing or blocking solutions). As a control, we stained Tango1i adipocytes, known to retain Collagen IV intracellularly (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011), and found that intracellularly retained Collagen IV could not be stained without permeabilization (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011

claim: Accumulations of Collagen IV in shii adipocytes were labeled without permeabilization, indicating that they were extracellular.
source: In contrast to this lack of staining, accumulations of Collagen IV in shii adipocytes were still labeled (Figure 2E), indicating that they were indeed extracellular.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Collagen IV accumulations in shii adipocytes are pericellular accumulations located outside of the PM.
source: Altogether, these data show that Collagen IV accumulations in shii adipocytes are pericellular accumulations located outside of the PM (see also electron micrographs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In mosaic experiments, accumulation of Vkg-GFP was suppressed when Vkg-GFP expression was knocked-down in the same cell.
source: Contradicting this hypothesis, however, we found in mosaic experiments that accumulation of Vkg-GFP was suppressed when Vkg-GFP expression was knocked-down in the same cell (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Collagen IV accumulated in a Dynamin-deficient adipocyte originates autonomously in that same cell.
source: This result demonstrates that Collagen IV accumulated in a Dynamin-deficient adipocyte originates autonomously in that same cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mosaic experiment data showing that knockdown of Vkg-GFP in the same cell suppresses accumulation

claim: Mosaic expression of Cg25C-RFP in shii adipocytes caused autonomous Collagen IV accumulation.
source: Supporting the autonomous origin of accumulated Collagen IV, mosaic expression of Cg25C-RFP (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in shii adipocytes caused autonomous Collagen IV accumulation as well (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Pericellularly accumulated Collagen IV is outgoing Collagen secreted by that same cell and becoming extracellularly trapped in the cell cortex.
source: These experiments indicate that Collagen IV pericellularly accumulating in a shii adipocyte is not Collagen that failed to be endocytosed. Contrary to that, our data show that pericellularly accumulated Collagen IV, instead of ingressing into the cell, is outgoing Collagen secreted by that same cell and becoming extracellularly trapped in the cell cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mosaic experiments and other data showing autonomous accumulation

claim: The endocytic marker TfR localized uniformly in the adipocyte PM and some intracellular vesicles.
source: The endocytic marker TfR (Transferrin Receptor, hTfR-GFP [Henthorn et al., 2011]) localized uniformly in the adipocyte PM and some intracellular vesicles (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and citation to Henthorn et al., 2011 for the TfR construct

claim: Knock-down of Rab11 caused TfR vesicles to fill the cytoplasm while no TfR was detected at the PM.
source: Confirming that TfR is internalized and recycled back to the PM, knock-down of Rab11, required for recycling endosome trafficking (Maxfield and McGraw, 2004), caused TfR vesicles to fill the cytoplasm while no TfR was detected at the PM (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J and citation to Maxfield and McGraw, 2004

claim: In Dynamin-deficient cells, TfR concentrated heavily in deep PM pockets containing Collagen IV at their center.
source: In Dynamin-deficient cells, in contrast, TfR concentrated heavily in deep PM pockets containing Collagen IV at their center (Figure 2I), suggesting that Collagen is pericellularly accumulated in PM pockets formed as a consequence of failed endocytosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Wild type adipocyte PM becomes somewhat convoluted in the third instar, displaying multiple invaginations which often encircle surface lipid droplets.
source: Wild type adipocyte PM, which is flat during the first and second larval instars, becomes somewhat convoluted in the third instar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), displaying multiple invaginations which often encircle surface lipid droplets (Diaconeasa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Diaconeasa et al., 2013

claim: Examination of endocytosis-deficient adipocytes revealed a striking increase in PM amount with respect to the wild type.
source: Compared to this, examination of endocytosis-deficient adipocytes revealed a striking increase in PM amount with respect to the wild type (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B

claim: Quantification in both confocal and electron micrographs showed an increase in the depth of PM ingression into the cytoplasm and higher PM sinuosity in endocytosis-defective cells.
source: Quantification in both confocal and electron micrographs showed an increase in the depth of PM ingression into the cytoplasm and higher PM sinuosity in endocytosis-defective cells (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: PM flattening, along with a vesicle-filled cytoplasm, resulted from Rab11 knock down.
source: The opposite phenotype, PM flattening, along with a vesicle-filled cytoplasm, resulted from Rab11 knock down.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Both endocytosis and membrane recycling are critical to maintain normal PM amount and cortical morphology.
source: These results indicate that both endocytosis and membrane recycling are critical to maintain normal PM amount and cortical morphology, suggesting that Collagen IV is trapped in an abnormally expanded cell cortex when endocytic removal of membrane from the PM is prevented.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing PM changes upon loss of endocytic and recycling components

claim: In larvae grown on lipid-depleted food, the amount of adipocyte PM was greatly reduced.
source: To confirm that an excessive amount of PM can act as a barrier to Collagen release after secretion, we aimed at artificially decreasing PM amount in adipocytes. To that end, we cultured flies in medium depleted of lipids through chloroform extraction (Palm et al., 2012). In larvae thus grown, we found that the amount of adipocyte PM was greatly reduced (Figure 3C,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citation to Palm et al., 2012 for the lipid depletion method

claim: Lipid-depleted food suppressed both PM excess and pericellular Collagen accumulation in Dynamin-deficient adipocytes.
source: Furthermore, lipid-depleted food suppressed both PM excess and pericellular Collagen accumulation in Dynamin-deficient adipocytes (Figure 3C,D), indicating that PM overgrowth was indeed responsible for pericellular Collagen trapping.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: PM excess resulting from lack of endocytic membrane removal leads to a hyperconvoluted PM, which in turn causes pericellular trapping of Collagen IV.
source: These data, in all, show that PM excess resulting from lack of endocytic membrane removal leads to a hyperconvoluted PM, which in turn causes pericellular trapping of Collagen IV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing PM changes and Collagen trapping

claim: Through iYFPi, Perlecan present in imaginal discs originated entirely in the fat body.
source: Through iYFPi (in vivo YFP interference, Figure 4A), we knocked down expression of Perlecan-YFP (trolCPTI-002049 [Rees et al., 2011]), a YFP-trap insertion predicted to label all Perlecan isoforms and found that Perlecan present in imaginal discs originated entirely in the fat body (Figure 4B), same as Collagen IV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B, and citation to Rees et al., 2011 for the Perlecan-YFP trap

claim: Trol-YFP was pericellularly accumulated in endocytosis-defective adipocytes.
source: Also similar to Collagen IV, Trol-YFP was pericellularly accumulated in endocytosis-defective adipocytes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: Accumulation of Trol (Perlecan) depended on Collagen IV, as it was suppressed by Collagen IV knock-down.
source: This accumulation of Trol (terribly reduced optic lobes) depended on Collagen IV, as it was suppressed by Collagen IV knock-down (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Nidogen accumulation was observed in endocytosis-defective adipocytes in a Collagen-dependent manner.
source: Through antibody staining, we confirmed Perlecan accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and additionally observed accumulation of Nidogen, again in a Collagen-dependent manner (Figure 5D), but not Laminin (anti-LanB1 staining, not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Laminin did not accumulate in endocytosis-defective adipocytes.
source: Through antibody staining, we confirmed Perlecan accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and additionally observed accumulation of Nidogen, again in a Collagen-dependent manner (Figure 5D), but not Laminin (anti-LanB1 staining, not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (anti-LanB1 staining)

claim: Vkg accumulation was suppressed by knock down of the Prolyl-4-hydroxylase PH4αEFB.
source: Indeed, Vkg accumulation was suppressed by knock down of the Prolyl-4-hydroxylase PH4αEFB (Figure 5E), in the absence of which Collagen IV is still secreted to the blood as non-functional monomeric chains (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011

claim: The secretion marker secr-GFP did not accumulate in the expanded cortex of shii adipocytes.
source: Additionally supporting the fibrotic nature of the deposits, the secretion marker secr-GFP (GFP coupled to a signal peptide [Pfeiffer et al., 2002]) did not accumulate in the expanded cortex of shii adipocytes (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2002 for the secr-GFP construct

claim: 26-29-protease and Ferritin 1HCH did not accumulate pericellularly upon shi knock down.
source: We also examined two other non-ECM proteins secreted by the fat body, 26-29-protease and Ferritin 1HCH, and none of them accumulated pericellularly upon shi knock down (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Not all proteins secreted by the fat body are pericellularly trapped as a result of PM overgrowth.
source: These results demonstrate that not all proteins secreted by the fat body are pericellularly trapped as a result of PM overgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing selective accumulation of ECM proteins but not other secreted proteins

claim: The aggregates consist of ECM proteins like trimeric Collagen IV, Perlecan and Nidogen, and thus are fibrotic deposits.
source: On the contrary, our data support the notion that the aggregates consist of ECM proteins like trimeric Collagen IV, Perlecan and Nidogen, and thus are fibrotic deposits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing accumulation of ECM proteins but not other secreted proteins

claim: Collagen IV is the main protein in the deposits, as accumulation of Perlecan and Nidogen depended on the presence of Collagen IV.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that Collagen IV is the main protein in this deposits, as accumulation of Perlecan and Nidogen depended on the presence of Collagen IV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Perlecan and Nidogen accumulation is suppressed by Collagen IV knockdown

claim: cactus knock-down causes pericellular Collagen accumulation in adipocytes.
source: Having established that extracellular deposits caused by PM overgrowth were not general protein aggregates but rather fibrotic ECM aggregates, we decided to investigate their wider biological effects. To do that, we first turned our attention to cactus, another PM accumulation hit in our screening (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: cact encodes a negative regulator of the Toll signaling pathway, a key mediator of innate immunity.
source: cactus (cact) encodes a negative regulator of the Toll signaling pathway, a key mediator of innate immunity (Roth et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roth et al., 1991

claim: Toll signaling is activated in cacti adipocytes as evidenced by Dorsal nuclear accumulation.
source: We confirmed activation of Toll signaling in cacti adipocytes (Dorsal nuclear accumulation) and further validated the phenotype by observing pericellular Collagen accumulation in cact4 mutants (Roth et al., 1991) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Roth et al., 1991 for the cact4 mutant

claim: cact4 mutants show pericellular Collagen accumulation.
source: We confirmed activation of Toll signaling in cacti adipocytes (Dorsal nuclear accumulation) and further validated the phenotype by observing pericellular Collagen accumulation in cact4 mutants (Roth et al., 1991) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Roth et al., 1991 for the cact4 mutant

claim: Expression of the constitutively active mutant receptor Toll10B produced pericellular Collagen accumulation.
source: Expression of the constitutively active mutant receptor Toll10B also produced pericellular Collagen accumulation (Figure 6B), as did infection with Toll-activating Gram+ bacteria Micrococcus luteus (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Infection with Toll-activating Gram+ bacteria Micrococcus luteus produced pericellular Collagen accumulation.
source: Expression of the constitutively active mutant receptor Toll10B also produced pericellular Collagen accumulation (Figure 6B), as did infection with Toll-activating Gram+ bacteria Micrococcus luteus (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Examination of cacti and Toll10B adipocytes revealed PM overgrowth, similar to shii adipocytes.
source: Examination of cacti and Toll10B adipocytes in confocal and electron micrographs revealed PM overgrowth (Figure 6D,E), similar to shii adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6E

claim: PM overgrowth upon Toll activation was suppressed by lipid-depleted food.
source: Also similar to shii adipocytes, PM overgrowth upon Toll activation was suppressed by lipid-depleted food (graph in Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Pericellular Collagen IV deposits upon Toll activation were extracellular.
source: Moreover, pericellular Collagen IV deposits were extracellular (antibody staining without permeabilization, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), disappeared upon PH4αEFB knock-down (Figure 6F) and did not contain secr-GFP (Figure 6G), but contained Perlecan (Figure 6H), indicating accumulation of fibrotic material, same as in endocytosis-defective cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Pericellular Collagen IV deposits upon Toll activation disappeared upon PH4αEFB knock-down.
source: Moreover, pericellular Collagen IV deposits were extracellular (antibody staining without permeabilization, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), disappeared upon PH4αEFB knock-down (Figure 6F) and did not contain secr-GFP (Figure 6G), but contained Perlecan (Figure 6H), indicating accumulation of fibrotic material, same as in endocytosis-defective cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Pericellular Collagen IV deposits upon Toll activation did not contain secr-GFP.
source: Moreover, pericellular Collagen IV deposits were extracellular (antibody staining without permeabilization, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), disappeared upon PH4αEFB knock-down (Figure 6F) and did not contain secr-GFP (Figure 6G), but contained Perlecan (Figure 6H), indicating accumulation of fibrotic material, same as in endocytosis-defective cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Pericellular Collagen IV deposits upon Toll activation contained Perlecan.
source: Moreover, pericellular Collagen IV deposits were extracellular (antibody staining without permeabilization, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), disappeared upon PH4αEFB knock-down (Figure 6F) and did not contain secr-GFP (Figure 6G), but contained Perlecan (Figure 6H), indicating accumulation of fibrotic material, same as in endocytosis-defective cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: No evidence of endocytosis/recycling defects was found when examining TfR-GFP localization in cacti and Toll10B adipocytes.
source: Despite these similarities with endocytosis-defective cells, we could not find evidence of endocytosis/recycling defects when we examined TfR-GFP localization in cacti and Toll10B adipocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that PM overgrowth upon Toll activation did not stem from reduced endocytosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Toll activation potently induces production of secreted antimicrobial peptides like Drosomycin, Defensin and Metchnikowin.
source: Toll activation, on the other hand, is known to potently induce production of secreted antimicrobial peptides like Drosomycin, Defensin and Metchnikowin (Lemaitre et al., 1996), which led as to consider increased secretion of these Toll targets as an alternative explanation to PM overgrowth upon Toll activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaitre et al., 1996

claim: Knock-down of Dif suppressed PM overgrowth in cacti and Toll10B adipocytes.
source: Consistent with this, knock-down of Dif, a transcription factor involved in expression of Toll target genes in the adult (Rutschmann et al., 2000) and larval fat body (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suppressed PM overgrowth (graph in Figure 6E) and pericellular Vkg-GFP trapping (not shown), suggesting that the transcriptional response to Toll activation contributed to Collagen IV accumulation in cacti and Toll10B adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and citation to Rutschmann et al., 2000

claim: The cytoplasm of cacti, Toll10B and M. luteus-infected adipocytes was filled with Drosomycin vesicles or granules.
source: Also consistent with a burst in secretory activity causing the PM overgrowth, the cytoplasm of cacti, Toll10B and M. luteus-infected adipocytes was filled with Drosomycin vesicles or granules (Figure 6I; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Knock-down of Rab1 caused abundant intracellular Drs-GFP retention in Toll10B adipocytes and suppression of PM excess.
source: Furthermore, knock-down of Rab1, required for ER-to-Golgi transport in the secretory pathway, caused not just abundant intracellular Drs-GFP retention in Toll10B adipocytes, but also suppression of PM excess (Figure 6J), implicating membrane input from the secretory pathway in PM overgrowth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J

claim: PM overgrowth and fibrotic deposits upon Toll activation result from increased secretory activity.
source: In all, our analysis indicates that PM overgrowth and fibrotic deposits upon Toll activation result from increased secretory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Dif knockdown effects, Drosomycin accumulation, and Rab1 knockdown effects

claim: 32 out of 70 hits producing pericellular Collagen IV accumulation showed clear signs of a fat body melanization response, including cact, shi, Rab5 and Chc.
source: In our screening, 32 out of 70 hits producing pericellular Collagen IV accumulation showed clear signs of a fat body melanization response, including cact, shi, Rab5 and Chc (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by screening data presented in Supplementary file 1

claim: Melanization is an insect immune response characterized by blackening of the affected tissue, usually accompanied by hemocyte (blood cell) recruitment.
source: Melanization is an insect immune response characterized by blackening of the affected tissue, usually accompanied by hemocyte (blood cell) recruitment (Minakhina and Steward, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Minakhina and Steward, 2006

claim: Melanization still occurred when using weaker fat body drivers ppl-GAL4 and r4-GAL4, inactive in blood cells.
source: Because BM-40-SPARC-GAL4 and Cg-GAL4, the strong fat body drivers we had used so far, are also expressed in blood cells, we tested weaker fat body drivers ppl-GAL4 and r4-GAL4, inactive in blood cells, and found that melanization still occurred (Figure 7A,B), ruling out that interfering with blood cell function caused the response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A and 7B

claim: Both the number of r4>shii larvae displaying melanization and the extent of it decreased when Collagen IV or PH4αEFB were additionally knocked down.
source: Furthermore, confirming the involvement of Collagen deposits in the response, both the number of r4>shii larvae displaying melanization and the extent of it decreased when we additionally knocked down Collagen IV or PH4αEFB (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D

claim: Reduction of Collagen IV and PH4αEFB reduced melanization of r4>Toll10B larvae.
source: Reduction of Collagen IV and PH4αEFB also reduced melanization of r4>Toll10B larvae (Figure 7D) and completely rescued their pupal lethality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Reduction of Collagen IV and PH4αEFB completely rescued pupal lethality of r4>Toll10B larvae.
source: Reduction of Collagen IV and PH4αEFB also reduced melanization of r4>Toll10B larvae (Figure 7D) and completely rescued their pupal lethality.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Collagen deposits either trigger or significantly contribute to fat body melanization in these conditions.
source: These results show that Collagen deposits either trigger or significantly contribute to fat body melanization in these conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Collagen IV knockdown reduces melanization

claim: shibire knock-down did not cause Toll pathway activation, as evidenced by lack of Drs-GFP induction and absence of nuclear Dorsal localization.
source: Given that Toll activation is long known to cause melanization (Gerttula et al., 1988), we examined Toll activity in shii adipocytes, but found that shibire knock-down did not cause Toll pathway activation, as evidenced by lack of Drs-GFP induction and absence of nuclear Dorsal localization (not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Drs-GFP and Dorsal localization assays) and citation to Gerttula et al., 1988

claim: Both shibire knockdown and Toll activation caused activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and Janus kinase/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (JAK/STAT) pathways.
source: In contrast, both shibire knockdown and Toll activation caused activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and Janus kinase/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (JAK/STAT) pathways, known to act together in response to tissue damage in other fly tissues (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Buchon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008 and Buchon et al., 2009

claim: JNK targets puckered (puc) and Matrix metallo-protease 1 (Mmp1) were induced in shii, Toll10B and cacti adipocytes.
source: JNK targets puckered (puc) and Matrix metallo-protease 1 (Mmp1) (Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006) were induced in shii, Toll10B and cacti adipocytes (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7E-G and citation to Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006

claim: The JAK/STAT reporter 10XSTAT-GFP was induced in shii, Toll10B and cacti adipocytes.
source: As for JAK/STAT signaling, we observed induction of the JAK/STAT reporter 10XSTAT-GFP (Ekas et al., 2006) (Figure 7G) and highly upregulated expression of unpaired 3 (upd3), encoding a JAK/STAT-activating cytokine (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and citation to Ekas et al., 2006 for the reporter

claim: Expression of unpaired 3 (upd3), encoding a JAK/STAT-activating cytokine, was highly upregulated in shii, Toll10B and cacti adipocytes.
source: As for JAK/STAT signaling, we observed induction of the JAK/STAT reporter 10XSTAT-GFP (Ekas et al., 2006) (Figure 7G) and highly upregulated expression of unpaired 3 (upd3), encoding a JAK/STAT-activating cytokine (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H

claim: Fibrotic deposits caused by endocytic defects or Toll provoke tissue damage in adipocytes and stimulate an innate immune response, as evidenced by tissue melanization, blood cell recruitment, activation of JAK/STAT signaling and JNK.
source: From these data, we conclude that fibrotic deposits caused by endocytic defects or Toll provoke tissue damage in adipocytes and stimulate an innate immune response, as evidenced by tissue melanization, blood cell recruitment, activation of JAK/STAT signaling and JNK (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing melanization, blood cell recruitment, and pathway activation; Figure 8 is referenced

claim: Collagen IV was effectively secreted and reached the extracellular space, but it was then trapped in fibrotic deposits at the cell periphery.
source: In investigating the cause for such a paradoxical phenotype, our experiments revealed that Collagen IV was effectively secreted and reached the extracellular space, but it was then trapped in fibrotic deposits at the cell periphery (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: Endocytic membrane removal and recycling are critical to maintain normal PM amount.
source: Further experiments led us to conclude that endocytic membrane removal and recycling are critical to maintain normal PM amount and that excess of PM when endocytic membrane removal was prevented resulted in a hyperconvoluted cell cortex where Collagen IV became entrapped (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: Excess of PM when endocytic membrane removal was prevented resulted in a hyperconvoluted cell cortex where Collagen IV became entrapped.
source: Further experiments led us to conclude that endocytic membrane removal and recycling are critical to maintain normal PM amount and that excess of PM when endocytic membrane removal was prevented resulted in a hyperconvoluted cell cortex where Collagen IV became entrapped (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: Both recycling endosome-derived and ER-derived membrane inputs may contribute to total PM amount while constant endocytic membrane removal prevents PM overgrowth.
source: Therefore, both recycling endosome-derived and ER-derived membrane inputs may contribute to total PM amount while constant endocytic membrane removal prevents PM overgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing effects of Rab11 and Rab1 knockdown

claim: A factor that might determine high PM turnover in adipocytes is their elevated secretory activity.
source: A factor that might determine high PM turnover in these cells, and thus a tendency to imbalances, is their elevated secretory activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known secretory function of adipocytes

claim: In Garland cells, shibire loss causes deep PM tubulation.
source: For instance, in Garland cells, a filtering cell type with high endocytic activity, shibire loss causes deep PM tubulation (Kosaka and Ikeda, 1983), whereas loss of Rab11 flattens the PM (Satoh et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kosaka and Ikeda, 1983 and Satoh et al., 2005

claim: In Garland cells, loss of Rab11 flattens the PM.
source: For instance, in Garland cells, a filtering cell type with high endocytic activity, shibire loss causes deep PM tubulation (Kosaka and Ikeda, 1983), whereas loss of Rab11 flattens the PM (Satoh et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Satoh et al., 2005

claim: In neurons, accumulation of membrane cisternae in synaptic boutons was observed upon Clathrin and Dynamin photoinactivation.
source: In neurons, accumulation of membrane cisternae in synaptic boutons was observed upon Clathrin and Dynamin photoinactivation (Heerssen et al., 2008; Kasprowicz et al., 2014), similar to the PM excess we found in adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Heerssen et al., 2008 and Kasprowicz et al., 2014

claim: Rab5 and other endocytic genes are required to maintain epithelial polarity.
source: Finally, Rab5 and other endocytic genes are required to maintain epithelial polarity (Lu and Bilder, 2005; Zeigerer et al., 2012), suggesting that constant endocytosis actively keeps apical and baso-lateral PMs segregated.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu and Bilder, 2005 and Zeigerer et al., 2012

claim: Constant endocytosis actively keeps apical and baso-lateral PMs segregated.
source: Finally, Rab5 and other endocytic genes are required to maintain epithelial polarity (Lu and Bilder, 2005; Zeigerer et al., 2012), suggesting that constant endocytosis actively keeps apical and baso-lateral PMs segregated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing endocytic genes are required for epithelial polarity

claim: Collagen IV self–interaction is critical in triggering pericellular aggregation.
source: That Collagen IV self–interaction is critical in triggering pericellular aggregation is indeed supported by the fact that knock-down of PH4α-EFB, required for trimer formation, suppresses aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that PH4α-EFB knockdown suppresses aggregates

claim: The size of the accumulated protein does not play a major role in the formation of the deposits.
source: In contrast, our data showing that PM surrounding aggregates can be stained equally well with both low (3000) and high (70,000) molecular weight fixable dextrans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggests that the size of the accumulated protein does not play a major role in the formation of the deposits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing equal staining with different molecular weight dextrans

claim: Perlecan does not accumulate by itself, but as a result of Collagen IV accumulation.
source: This is also supported by the finding that Perlecan, a large 400 kDa protein, does not accumulate by itself, but as a result of Collagen IV accumulation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Loss of BM-40-SPARC causes Collagen IV deposits on adipocytes.
source: Loss of BM-40-SPARC, one of these hits, was previously known to cause Collagen IV deposits on adipocytes (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011

claim: Other basement membrane components accumulate upon loss of BM-40-SPARC.
source: Furthermore, similar to the fibrotic deposits in our study, other basement membrane components accumulate upon loss of BM-40-SPARC (Shahab et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahab et al., 2015

claim: The PM is not overgrown in BM-40-SPARCi adipocytes.
source: However, the PM is not overgrown in BM-40-SPARCi adipocytes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the way in which aggregates form in BM-40-SPARCi adipocytes is different from the way they arise in endocytosis-defective and Toll-activated adipocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: None of the PM accumulation hits (except cactus) causes Collagen IV deposits through ectopic Toll activation.
source: We have also tested Toll pathway activation by examining expression of Toll target Drosomycin (Drs-GFP) in BM-40-SPARCi and all other PM accumulation hits, but found no Drosomycin-GFP induction in any of them. This suggests that, cactus aside, none of the hits causes Collagen IV deposits through ectopic Toll activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Drs-GFP expression assays)

claim: Aspects of the response to pericellular Collagen trapping include melanization and activation of the JAK/STAT and JNK pathways.
source: Pericellular trapping of Collagen IV, apart from preventing its incorporation to destination tissues, induces a potent response in adipocytes. Aspects of this response include melanization and activation of the JAK/STAT and JNK pathways (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: Concomitant activation of JNK and JAK/STAT signaling makes this response reminiscent of tissue damage responses in imaginal discs and gut tissues.
source: Concomitant activation of JNK and JAK/STAT signaling makes this response reminiscent of tissue damage responses in imaginal discs and gut tissues (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Buchon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008 and Buchon et al., 2009

claim: Predominance of upd3 among induced JAK/STAT cytokines is shared with the intestinal response to tissue damage.
source: In particular, predominance of upd3 among induced JAK/STAT cytokines is shared with the intestinal response to tissue damage (Buchon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buchon et al., 2009

claim: It has been suggested that basement membrane disruption could be a signal that intestinal cells sense when flies are fed tissue damage-inducing Dextran Sulfate Sodium.
source: It has been suggested that basement membrane disruption could be a signal that intestinal cells sense when flies are fed tissue damage-inducing Dextran Sulfate Sodium (Amcheslavsky et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amcheslavsky et al., 2009

claim: Absence of basement membrane has been linked to melanization as a permissive factor.
source: Absence of basement membrane, although unable by itself to elicit a response (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008), has been recently linked to melanization as a permissive factor (Hauling et al., 2014; Kim and Choe, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008, Hauling et al., 2014, and Kim and Choe, 2014

claim: It is the fibrotic deposits that cause the response rather than absence of a basement membrane, since Collagen IV knock down in shii cells suppressed the response instead of enhancing it.
source: In the case of adipocyte fibrosis, however, our data indicate that it is the fibrotic deposits that cause the response rather than absence of a basement membrane, since Collagen IV knock down in shii cells suppressed the response instead of enhancing it.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Collagen IV knockdown suppresses the response

claim: Even though Toll targets include melanization enzymes, Collagen deposits contribute to Toll-induced melanization.
source: Also in Toll10B adipocytes, Collagen IV reduction partially suppressed melanization, showing that, even though Toll targets include melanization enzymes (De Gregorio et al., 2002), Collagen deposits contribute to Toll-induced melanization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Collagen IV reduction suppresses melanization, and citation to De Gregorio et al., 2002

claim: Adipocyte fibrosis in humans and mouse models is correlated with obesity and adipose tissue dysfunction.
source: Adipocyte fibrosis in humans and mouse models is correlated with obesity and adipose tissue dysfunction (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2013

claim: Human adipocytes are surrounded by a basement membrane containing Collagen IV.
source: Same as human adipocytes, Drosophila larval adipocytes are surrounded by a basement membrane containing Collagen IV (Chun, 2012); also similar, human adipocytes display complex PM topology, with abundant caveolae forming higher-level rosettes (Fan et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chun, 2012

claim: Human adipocytes display complex PM topology, with abundant caveolae forming higher-level rosettes.
source: Same as human adipocytes, Drosophila larval adipocytes are surrounded by a basement membrane containing Collagen IV (Chun, 2012); also similar, human adipocytes display complex PM topology, with abundant caveolae forming higher-level rosettes (Fan et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 1983

claim: Fibrosis is thought to result in all cases from inflammatory stimulation of excess ECM deposition.
source: Fibrosis, affecting adipocytes or otherwise, is thought to result in all cases from inflammatory stimulation of excess ECM deposition.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about fibrosis

claim: Accumulation of trimeric Collagen IV can be triggered by Toll immune activation and deposits in turn further stimulate other arms of the fly immune system different from the Toll-mediated immune response.
source: Our results show that accumulation of trimeric Collagen IV can be triggered by Toll immune activation and that deposits in turn further stimulate other arms of the fly immune system different from the Toll-mediated immune response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Toll activation causes deposits and deposits activate JAK/STAT and JNK

claim: Fibrotic accumulations, once initiated, could be self-sustained, with inflammation and fibrosis feeding each other.
source: This raises the possibility that fibrotic accumulations, once initiated, could be self-sustained, with inflammation and fibrosis feeding each other.
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding that Toll activation causes deposits and deposits activate immune responses

claim: The response to fibrosis includes induction of Collagen-degrading enzyme Matrix metalloprotease 1, suggesting that the response is aimed in part at clearing the aggregates.
source: Interestingly, the response to fibrosis includes induction of Collagen-degrading enzyme Matrix metalloprotease 1, suggesting that the response is aimed in part at clearing the aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Mmp1 induction
